subject: Optimizing the posterior and warmup sampling

messages.author: 2edec1f5143b1fb5
messages.subject: Optimizing the posterior and warmup sampling
parts:
Hello,

I am a PhD student in Civil Engineering at the University of Colorado at Boulder.  Last semester I fulfilled my final coursework credit by taking a spatial statistics course.  For the final project in this class, I had built a Bayesian stochastic weather generator in Stan (and RStan).  A quick description of this model is as follows:

I have daily weather (precipitation, temperature) data for 15 stations in Argentina.  I am using probit regression for the precipitation occurrence, and gamma for the intensity; the temperature processes (minimum and maximum) are conditioned on precipitation occurrence, previous day's temperature, and are modeled using linear regression.  What I have done is set up the model so each location has spatially-correlated coefficients for their respective regressions, each coefficient with respective kriging parameters (assumed no nugget [they are latent processes], variable sill, and variable range).  In the model file, the errors for each of the models are not assumed to be spatially correlated.  

For my class, I ran eight chains of the model in parallel, each with 1400 iterations; the warmup period for each chain is 1000.  The results looked very good -- the model converged well before the end of the warmup period, and I had 3200 samples making up the posterior distributions, which had properties consistent with convergence.  I did not simulate daily weather on a grid, so did not use the spatial parameters to simulate the regression coefficients on a grid.  My multisite simulations looked very good.

Now this model has become a potential chapter of my dissertation, and I have begun using conditional simulation (sim.Krig in the fields package) to simulate the regression coefficients on a regular grid.  These daily weather sequences will be used by scientists and agronomists in Argentina to drive hydrologic and crop simulation models for better estimates of risk on the seasonal scale.  Naturally, I used the model I built and subsequently ran for my spatial statistics class as a first go for simulating these gridded weather sequences.  It turns out the estimation of sill and range (which, unfortunately, are inconsistently estimable) are wrong, which was due to the fact that I set a maximum limit on the range to be the maximum distance between stations.  This in turn lead to incorrect estimates of both sill and range, and produced wildly (spatially) variable coefficients.

I have met with a colleague, who thinks it is physically unrealistic to set this maximum bound on the range parameter.  After going back through my model and setting a very large maximum limit (1000x the maximum distance between stations), I was able to optimize the posterior and obtain the mode for each parameter.  Indeed, the optimal range values are more than 2x the maximum distance between stations (this is a small basin, and the range parameter is for unobserved processes -- the coefficients).  Using these optimized parameters to simulate gridded weather sequences yields reasonable results.  However, using the modes for these parameters as initial guesses in my updated Stan model, and inflating the max_treedepth value to 20 (as is suggested for big models), my model simply sits at the first iteration during warmup.  I figured I would let it run for a while to see if it ever got past the first iteration, to no avail.  It was still on the first iteration after nearly 2 days, at which point I had to kill the job.

Can you advise on the situation?  I have attached my model, R script, and data files (NOTE: the .RData file needed to load setup information would not attach to this post.  You may access this through my ftp site at http://civil.colorado.edu/~verdina/20140930-gridSim-setup-oneyear-oneTempCov.RData )

Thanks!
Andrew Verdin

messages.author: f13fe7e880ed6103
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimizing the posterior and warmup sampling
parts:
In your R script, it looks like you're transforming your initial values:

pars = function()constrain_pars(stan_model,o$par)

But if o$par contains the true parameter values in unlogged space, I think you can pass those directly to Stan, i.e.:

sflist <- stan(fit = stan_model, data = lm_data,
                chains = 1, iter=iterations, init=list(o$par),
                seed = rng_seed, warmup = warmup, refresh = 1, control=list(max_treedepth=20))

(Another thing I'd try is rerunning with 4 chains rather than just 1, but maybe you've tried that already.)

Next thing I'd do is to try a non-zero nugget. This may not be correct for your setting theoretically, but it helps in practice with numerical stability. You could replace all the calls to exp_cov_matrix(..., 0) with, e.g. exp_cov_matrix(..., 0.0001).

Other suggestions that won't necessarily help with your issue but aren't a bad idea in any case (and might uncover a bug):

        c_max <- exp_cov_matrix(x, sill, range, nugget)

can be replaced with

       c_max <- sill * exp(-1.0 / range * x);
       for(i in 1:M)
             c_max[i,i] <- sill + nugget;

Another quick thing to try is that I've had more success using an inverse sqrt length-scale specification:

c_max <- sill * exp(- invrange * x[i,j])

I'm having trouble getting your code to run, perhaps because I'm missing some libraries. If you can simplify things a bit--trying fixing some of the parameters, using fewer weather stations, conditioning on fewer variables, etc.--and also send code that's easier to run, i.e. if possible the R code should just load an RData file and then compile and run the model, that'll help us give you more ideas...

Seth
P.S. Here's what happens when I try to run your code:

> o = readRDS("spatial-wgen-nonugget-largerange-optimpars.rds") # this doesn't throw a warning or error 
> o$par$sigma2_max  # did it load correctly?
Error in o$par$sigma2_max : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors

I am constraining the optimized parameters because before I optimized these values, I unconstrained them using unconstrain_pars(stan_model, pars()). I didn't clarify this, and I apologize for that.  

What would running 4 chains (as opposed to 1 chain) do differently?  I typically run only one chain when I am testing and debugging my models.

I've attached updated versions of the files that I included in my original post.  (Again, the RData file would not attach to this thread... so it can be found at http://civil.colorado.edu/~verdina/bayes-wgen-stanlist.RData ).  As suggested, I have amended the R script so it simply reads in an RData file, compiles the model, and runs.

Thanks again for your help!

Best,
Andrew Verdin

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimizing the posterior and warmup sampling
parts: The advantage of running 4 chains rather than 1 is that you can easily diagnose convergence. With only 1 chain it’s hard to tell what’s going on. Especially when testing and debugging when you’re trying different things. You might be able to run 4 chains for 100 iterations each instead of nervously running 1 chain for 2000 iterations, for example.

>
> What would running 4 chains (as opposed to 1 chain) do differently? I typically run only one chain when I am testing and debugging my models.
>

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Optimizing the posterior and warmup sampling
parts:
You might want to try running with a smaller initial step size
(control=list(stepsize=0.01) in R) to see if that helps.

The random init with a variable constrained (0,20) is going
to be around 10. We usually recommend not putting the hard
constraint (0,20) on things like scale parameters, but rather
a weakly informative prior that concentrates mass mostly where we
expect it but allows for any value with enough data.

You may be having similar problems with those other interval-constrained
parameters.

- Bob
